publication.title: From disengagement to regional war: Israel, Gaza and the Middle East since 2005
publication.summary: A dated sequence from Gaza disengagement and Hamas rule through conflict cycles, Hezbollah, Iran's partner network, the Abraham Accords, October 7, the Gaza and Lebanon wars, the Red Sea front and direct Iran–Israel confrontation. Current judgments remain explicitly provisional.
publication.body:
The period since 2005 did not move in one direction. Israel left its settlements and permanent ground presence in Gaza, Hamas won an election and then seized exclusive control there, repeated wars hardened separation, and regional diplomacy expanded even as Iran-linked armed groups and direct state conflict widened the battlefield. October 7 and the war that followed transformed every earlier trend. Current events remain provisional history: responsibility and consequence can be documented before a final regional verdict is possible.

2005 — disengagement. Israel evacuated all settlements in Gaza and four in the northern West Bank and withdrew its permanent forces from inside the Strip. The government described the move as unilateral, intended to improve security and reduce responsibility in the absence of a negotiating partner. Palestinians gained freedom from settlements and permanent Israeli deployment inside Gaza but not sovereign control over airspace, maritime access, most crossings, population registry and much external movement. Israel says occupation ended; the UN, ICRC and most international legal authorities continued to treat Gaza as occupied because of effective external control. The legal dispute does not change what was removed or what controls remained.

The disengagement was not a peace agreement. It did not settle borders, refugees, Jerusalem, security or relations between Gaza and the West Bank. Supporters argued that it removed civilians and soldiers from an indefensible deployment. Critics on the Israeli right said withdrawal under fire rewarded armed groups; Palestinian critics said unilateralism entrenched Israeli control elsewhere. Later events are evidence about consequences, but they do not prove that every outcome was inevitable in 2005.

2006–2007 — election and takeover. Hamas won the January 2006 Palestinian legislative election, defeating Fatah after campaigning on resistance, governance and corruption. International donors demanded recognition of Israel, renunciation of violence and acceptance of prior agreements. Palestinian factional conflict escalated. In June 2007, Hamas forces seized Palestinian Authority security installations and established de facto control in Gaza, while a Fatah-led Palestinian Authority remained in the West Bank.

Election victory and armed takeover are separate events. The first provided electoral legitimacy for a legislature and government; the second produced exclusive territorial rule after violent conflict. No national election subsequently renewed either Hamas's Gaza mandate or the Palestinian Authority presidency. The political split weakened Palestinian representation and made one diplomatic address for Gaza and the West Bank increasingly difficult.

Blockade and conflict cycles. After Hamas's takeover and continuing rocket fire, Israel imposed far-reaching restrictions on goods and movement, with Egypt also controlling its border. Israel described the restrictions as security measures against weapons and attacks; humanitarian organizations documented deep effects on civilian movement, health, infrastructure and the economy. The degree to which Gaza remained occupied, the legality of blockade measures and the responsibilities of Hamas, Israel and Egypt remain contested, but civilian dependence and recurring insecurity are observable facts.

Major escalations followed in 2008–09, 2012, 2014 and 2021, with additional shorter rounds. Hamas and other groups fired rockets indiscriminately toward Israeli population centers and built tunnels and military infrastructure. Israel conducted air and ground campaigns against those capabilities in a densely populated enclave. Investigations repeatedly alleged unlawful conduct by different parties. Each round ended without resolving governance, blockade, disarmament, reconstruction or political sovereignty.

The Hezbollah era. Hezbollah's growth combined Lebanese politics and social institutions with an armed organization supported by Iran. Israel withdrew from its southern Lebanon occupation zone in 2000. Hezbollah's July 2006 cross-border attack and capture of Israeli soldiers triggered a war that caused extensive casualties, displacement and infrastructure damage in Lebanon and attacks on Israeli civilians. Security Council Resolution 1701 called for cessation of hostilities, Lebanese state and UNIFIL deployment in the south, Israeli withdrawal and an area free of unauthorized armed personnel and weapons.

Resolution 1701 constrained but did not eliminate the conflict. Hezbollah retained and expanded a large arsenal; Israel conducted surveillance and strikes it linked to weapons transfers and threats; Lebanon's state lacked exclusive control of force. The calm along much of the border was therefore deterrence under an incompletely implemented resolution, not reconciliation.

Iran's regional relationships. Iran supported Hezbollah, Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, the Houthis and named Iraqi armed groups through different combinations of finance, weapons, training and political alignment. The evidence does not support treating every organization as a remote-controlled unit. Resource dependence, strategic alignment, consultation, operational cooperation and command are different levels. Local actors retain constituencies and objectives even when Iranian support is decisive.

The Abraham Accords. Beginning in 2020, Israel established or renewed formal relations with the UAE, Bahrain and Morocco, while Sudan signed the general declaration but did not complete normalization. The agreements expanded trade, travel, technology and security cooperation and reflected shared concern about Iran as well as national interests. They also bypassed the assumption that Israeli–Palestinian peace had to precede wider Arab normalization. Palestinians saw that sequence as abandonment; advocates argued regional ties could create new incentives and practical gains.

October 7, 2023. Hamas-led attackers crossed from Gaza into southern Israel, killed civilians and security personnel, committed hostage-taking and other grave abuses, and took hostages into Gaza. The attack exposed major Israeli intelligence, military and political failures and shattered the assumption that Hamas could be contained through deterrence and economic management. Evidence for particular atrocities must still be assessed claim by claim; correcting an unsupported detail does not diminish the documented scale or intent of the assault.

The Gaza war. Israel stated goals of destroying Hamas's military and governing capacity and returning hostages. Its campaign killed Hamas commanders and fighters and destroyed military infrastructure, but also killed very large numbers of Palestinian civilians, displaced most of Gaza's population and devastated homes, health systems and basic services. Casualty classifications, proportionality assessments and legal responsibility remain disputed and are subject to judicial and investigative processes. The facts of mass civilian harm and Hamas's embedding of military activity among civilians can coexist; neither automatically resolves the legality of a specific strike.

Hostages, aid and governance became connected fronts. Negotiations produced temporary releases and ceasefires but repeatedly failed to settle the war's end state. Israel faced the problem of replacing Hamas without indefinite military government; Palestinians faced catastrophic survival conditions and fragmented political authority. International actors disagreed over recognition, reconstruction, security guarantees and whether any postwar arrangement could revive a two-state process.

The Lebanon front after October 7. Hezbollah began attacks across the border on October 8, saying it was supporting Gaza. Israel returned fire and later expanded operations; communities on both sides were displaced. Escalation weakened Hezbollah's senior leadership and military infrastructure but did not erase the organization or solve the Lebanese state's sovereignty problem. Subsequent ceasefire arrangements and renewed strikes must be dated separately. Current September 2026 reporting shows another active escalation, with casualty claims and target descriptions still requiring source-by-source verification.

The Red Sea and Yemen. The Houthis attacked commercial shipping and launched missiles and drones toward Israel, describing the campaign as solidarity with Gaza. Many affected vessels had weak or no direct Israeli connection. U.S., British, Israeli and partner strikes sought to protect navigation and degrade capabilities while Yemen's long war and humanitarian crisis continued. Bab al-Mandeb disruption rerouted trade and raised costs; it also demonstrated how a local armed movement can impose global economic effects without controlling the entire maritime route.

Direct Iran–Israel confrontation. A shadow conflict of covert action, cyber operations and strikes on Iranian-linked personnel moved into overt state-to-state exchanges beginning in 2024 and expanded in subsequent confrontations. Official claims about interceptions, damage and retaliation are evidence of what governments said and did, but wartime assessments of effectiveness require independent imagery, casualty records and dated operational evidence. Current reports concerning Hormuz, U.S. forces and Iran-aligned groups should not be retroactively merged into one centrally ordered campaign.

Regional realignment. Israel's partnerships with several Arab governments, U.S. security commitments, Iranian alliances and Turkey's and Gulf states' changing roles now overlap with the unresolved Palestinian conflict. Saudi–Israeli normalization has been discussed but should not be written as completed. The Gaza war increased public and diplomatic costs for normalization even where state security cooperation persisted. Iran's partners have suffered losses yet retain independent capacity; calling the network either destroyed or fully unified goes beyond the record.

What changed structurally. The Israeli–Palestinian arena and the regional arena can no longer be narrated separately. Gaza affects Red Sea shipping, Lebanese security, U.S.–Iran confrontation and Arab diplomacy. At the same time, a regional connection does not establish one command chain. The correct unit of analysis changes by claim: a treaty, a supply route, an attack order, a local decision, an election or a civilian consequence.

What remains unsettled. The political future of Gaza, Palestinian representation, hostage and prisoner arrangements, Lebanese state control, Hezbollah's arsenal, Iran's deterrence strategy, Saudi normalization and accountability for wartime conduct remain open. A history chapter can document decisions and their immediate effects. It should retain revision markers and resist presenting today's coalition map as the final regional order.

research.conclusion: Publish a chronological companion distinguishing disengagement from sovereignty, election from takeover, relationships from command, ceasefires from peace and current reporting from settled history. The account dates the September 2026 material and avoids declaring Saudi normalization, regional order or final war outcomes complete.

siteRecommendations: RUN 27 STATIC INTEGRATION GAP: the companion is not incorporated into /israels-story. Acceptance: add a 2005-to-current chapter sequence with visible last-checked dates on open events and durable links to canonical developing records rather than copying their changing casualty lines.

RUN 27 PROVISIONALITY: October 7 investigations, Gaza casualty classifications and legal findings, postwar governance, Lebanon ceasefire implementation, Houthi capability, Iranian command relationships and direct-war damage remain contested or developing. Acceptance: preserve prior assessments and show dated revisions when evidence changes.

RUN 27 SOURCE GAP: a permanent rebuild should attach the 2006 Palestinian election observer report, claim-level Gaza-war incident records, authoritative hostage and casualty datasets, and each current ceasefire text. Do not infer completeness from the public article inventory.
